u7.intro: Every excerpt is paraphrased and labelled with its source, and the table gives rounded figures. Answer from the sources and from what you know of the period 1890 to 1945.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-3 refer to the two excerpts below.

Source 1
The Philippines are ours forever, and just beyond them lie China's boundless markets. We will retreat from neither. We will not renounce our part in the mission of our race, trustee under God of the civilization of the world. The Filipinos are not a self-governing race and are not capable of becoming one. God has not been preparing the English-speaking and Teutonic peoples for a thousand years for nothing but idle self-admiration; He has made us the master organizers of the world, to establish system where chaos reigns.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from Senator Albert J. Beveridge of Indiana, speech in the U.S. Senate, January 9, 1900. The wording is not a direct quotation.

Source 2
We hold that the policy known as imperialism is hostile to liberty and tends toward militarism, an evil from which it has been our glory to be free. We regret that it has become necessary, in the land of Washington and Lincoln, to reaffirm that all men, of whatever race or color, are entitled to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed. We insist that the subjugation of any people is criminal aggression. We denounce the slaughter of the Filipinos as a needless horror, and we deplore the sacrifice of our soldiers in an unjust war.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from the platform of the American Anti-Imperialist League, adopted at Chicago, October 1899. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes the central disagreement between the two sources?
(A) Whether American businesses should compete for new markets in China and elsewhere in Asia
(B) Whether the United States had been right to go to war with Spain to free Cuba in 1898
(C) Whether government by consent of the governed must extend to peoples acquired overseas
(D) Whether English-speaking peoples were better fitted than other peoples to organize and govern
parts.a: (C). Source 1 justifies ruling Filipinos on the ground that they are 'not capable' of self-government, so their consent is irrelevant; Source 2 answers that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed and that this right belongs to people 'of whatever race or color.' The quarrel is over whether American principles follow the flag. (A) Source 1 mentions China's markets, but Source 2 says nothing against trade; it objects to ruling people without their consent, so markets are not the point in dispute. (B) Neither source discusses Cuba. The war Source 2 condemns is the 'unjust war' against the Filipinos, which followed the war with Spain. (D) Source 1 asserts this, but Source 2 never denies it; it argues that rights do not depend on race. Many anti-imperialists in fact shared racial views, which is why the disagreement is about consent, not about racial capacity.
parts.n: KC-7.3.I.A and KC-7.3.I.B (topic 7.2), skill 3.C. Thinking: find the premise each side argues from, not every topic one side mentions. Trap: (D) reads Source 2's phrase "of whatever race or color" as a denial of racial hierarchy, when it is a claim about rights.

parts.q:
Source 2's warning that imperialism 'tends toward militarism' drew most directly on which development at the time the platform was adopted?
(A) The dispatch of American troops to help put down the Boxer Rebellion in northern China
(B) The U.S. Army's war against Filipino nationalists led by Emilio Aguinaldo
(C) The building of a canal across the Isthmus of Panama under American control
(D) The sinking of the USS Maine in Havana harbor and the naval battles that followed
parts.a: (B). In October 1899 American troops were fighting Filipino nationalists who had declared independence; the platform denounces 'the slaughter of the Filipinos' and 'an unjust war,' the conflict KC-7.3.I.C calls the suppression of a nationalist movement. (A) The Boxer uprising and the relief expedition to Beijing came in the summer of 1900, after the platform was written, and the source names the Filipinos. (C) Construction of the Panama Canal began in 1904, years after the platform, and involved no war the platform could have denounced. (D) The Maine sank in February 1898 and the war with Spain was over by August 1898; the platform condemns a war being fought in 1899.
parts.n: KC-7.3.I.C (topic 7.3), skill 4.B. Thinking: date the source and match its complaint to the war under way when it was written. Trap: (D) links "militarism" to the best-known episode of 1898 without checking that the source is dated October 1899.

parts.q:
A historian argues that the anti-imperialist movement was united by the belief, stated in Source 2, that the rights of the Declaration of Independence belong to all people 'of whatever race or color.' Which of the following would most weaken this argument?
(A) The Senate ratified the Treaty of Paris in February 1899 by only one vote more than the two-thirds majority required.
(B) The Anti-Imperialist League's members included the industrialist Andrew Carnegie and the writer Mark Twain.
(C) Imperialists such as Beveridge argued that the islands would open the markets of Asia to American goods.
(D) Some prominent opponents of annexation objected that it would bring millions of nonwhite people into the nation.
parts.a: (D). If prominent anti-imperialists opposed annexation because they did not want nonwhite peoples inside the nation, then racial exclusion, not racial equality, moved part of the coalition; KC-7.3.I.B notes that anti-imperialists invoked racial theories as well as self-determination. (A) The narrow vote shows how divided the Senate was, not why opponents of annexation opposed it. (B) A list of famous members shows the breadth of the coalition but says nothing about whether its members shared a belief in racial equality. (C) This describes the imperialists' motives; the argument being tested is about what united their opponents.
parts.n: KC-7.3.I.B (topic 7.2), skill 3.D. Thinking: test a claim about a whole movement against evidence about the motives of some of its members. Trap: (A) treats the close Senate vote as evidence about motives because it is the most specific fact offered.

mc.stem:
Questions 4-6 refer to the two excerpts below.

Historian A
The leaders of Progressive reform came largely from an older middle class of lawyers, ministers, editors, professors and small-town businessmen. Around 1900 these people were not poorer than before, but they had lost standing: the new industrial millionaires eclipsed them in wealth, and the city political machines, resting on immigrant votes, eclipsed them in power. Their crusades against the trusts and the bosses expressed a wish to restore the influence of people like themselves as much as a wish to help the poor.

Paraphrase of the 'status revolution' argument in Richard Hofstadter, The Age of Reform (1955), condensed for this exercise. The wording is not a direct quotation.

Historian B
The regulation of the Progressive Era was not forced on big business against its will. The heads of the largest corporations, unable to control prices and competition through mergers alone, turned to the federal government to stabilize their industries. Much of the legislation passed in the name of the people was shaped by the businessmen it was meant to regulate, and it protected established firms from smaller competitors and from more radical state laws.

Paraphrase of the argument in Gabriel Kolko, The Triumph of Conservatism (1963), condensed for this exercise. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q:
The two historians differ most directly over which of the following questions?
(A) Which social group drove Progressive reform, and whose interests the reforms served
(B) Whether Progressive regulation actually reduced the power of the largest corporations
(C) Whether Progressive reform was a response to the rise of industrial capitalism
(D) Whether the states or the federal government led the way in Progressive reform
parts.a: (A). Historian A traces reform to an older middle class seeking to recover its lost standing; Historian B traces the federal regulation of the era to big businessmen seeking stability and protection from competitors. They answer 'who drove reform, and for whom?' differently. (B) Historian B implies it did not, but Historian A's excerpt makes no claim about results; it explains who led reform and why, so this is not the point on which they divide. (C) Both agree on this: Historian A points to 'industrial millionaires' and Historian B to the largest corporations. A shared premise is not a disagreement. (D) Historian B mentions both federal law and 'radical state laws,' but Historian A says nothing about the level of government, so the excerpts do not disagree on it.
parts.n: KC-7.1.II.A and KC-7.1.II.B (topic 7.4), skill 3.C. Thinking: separate what each historian claims from what only one of them addresses. Trap: (B) notices that Historian B doubts the reforms' effect and assumes Historian A must have claimed the opposite.

parts.q:
Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support Historian B's argument?
(A) Upton Sinclair's The Jungle sold widely among middle-class readers horrified by conditions in the packinghouses.
(B) Ida Tarbell's magazine articles exposed the ruthless methods Standard Oil had used to crush its smaller competitors.
(C) The largest meatpacking firms backed federal inspection in 1906, expecting a government seal to help their exports.
(D) Women in the settlement houses lobbied city governments for playgrounds, sanitation and factory inspection.
parts.a: (C). If the biggest packers wanted federal inspection because a government seal would reopen export markets, and the public paid the cost, then the regulated industry helped shape its own regulation for its own ends: exactly Historian B's claim. This is the example Kolko himself used. (A) The novel's middle-class audience points to public pressure from outside business, which fits Historian A better; it does not show the packers shaping the law. (B) Muckraking against a trust shows reformers attacking big business, the opposite of Historian B's picture of business sponsoring regulation. (D) Middle-class women reformers acting in cities support Historian A's emphasis on the middle class, not Historian B's on big business.
parts.n: KC-7.1.II.B (topic 7.4), skill 3.D. Thinking: decide which piece of evidence shows the regulated industry itself wanting the regulation. Trap: (A) picks the best-known cause of the 1906 meat law without asking whose interests the evidence shows.

parts.q:
Both historians place the driving force of reform outside the urban immigrant working class. Which of the following would most seriously challenge that shared view?
(A) Theodore Roosevelt, a wealthy New Yorker, campaigned in 1912 for federal commissions to regulate the largest corporations.
(B) After the 1911 Triangle fire, Tammany politicians Robert Wagner and Al Smith led a factory inquiry that won safety laws.
(C) Jane Addams and other college-educated women founded Hull House to serve immigrant families in Chicago.
(D) Governor Robert La Follette relied on university experts to draft Wisconsin laws on railroads and taxes.
parts.a: (B). Wagner, a German-born immigrant, and Smith, a grandson of immigrants raised on the Lower East Side, were products of the very Tammany machine that Historian A's reformers fought. Their Factory Investigating Commission produced a wave of New York labor and safety laws, which suggests that working-class voters and their machine politicians drove some Progressive reform. (A) A wealthy reformer promising federal regulation of big business fits both historians' pictures; it challenges neither. (C) Immigrants appear here as the people reformers served, not as the reformers; educated middle-class women leading reform fit Historian A. (D) Reliance on professional experts fits Historian A's professional middle class and the Progressive faith in expertise (KC-7.1.II.D); it does not point to working-class leadership.
parts.n: KC-7.1.II.A and KC-7.1.II.D (topic 7.4), skill 6.D. Thinking: find evidence that falls outside both interpretations rather than evidence that fits one of them. Trap: (C) sees "immigrant families" and misses that the immigrants are the people served, not the people leading reform.

mc.stem:
Questions 7-9 refer to the excerpt below.

On the first of February the Imperial German Government announced that it would put aside all restraints and use its submarines to sink every vessel that sought to approach the ports of Great Britain and Ireland or the western coasts of Europe. Vessels of every kind, whatever their flag or their errand, have been sent to the bottom without warning, American ships and American lives among them. The present German submarine warfare against commerce is a warfare against all nations. There is one choice we cannot make: we will not choose the path of submission. We have no selfish ends to serve; we desire no conquest and no dominion. The world must be made safe for democracy. We shall fight for the rights of nations great and small, and for a universal dominion of right by such a concert of free peoples as shall bring peace and safety to all nations.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from President Woodrow Wilson, address to a joint session of Congress, April 2, 1917. The wording is not a direct quotation, except the sentence 'The world must be made safe for democracy.'

parts.q:
Based on the excerpt, which of the following best explains why the United States declared war in 1917 rather than in 1915, when a German submarine sank the British liner Lusitania?
(A) No American citizens had died on the Lusitania, so its sinking gave the United States no legal grounds for war.
(B) The Russian Revolution had already taken Russia out of the war, leaving the Allies near defeat in the east.
(C) Congress had just repealed the Neutrality Acts that barred Wilson from selling weapons to the Allies.
(D) Germany had broken its pledge to limit submarine attacks and now threatened all ships, American ones included.
parts.a: (D). The excerpt stresses that Germany 'put aside all restraints' on February 1, 1917. After the Lusitania (1915) and the Sussex (1916) Germany had promised to stop sinking merchant ships without warning; the return to unrestricted submarine warfare against every flag is what turned protest into war. (A) About 128 Americans died on the Lusitania. Wilson protested sharply, and Germany eventually pledged restraint; the difference in 1917 is that the pledge was abandoned. (B) Russia left the war only after the Bolsheviks seized power in November 1917 and made a separate peace in March 1918, both after the United States declared war. (C) The Neutrality Acts date from 1935 to 1937. In 1914-1917 Americans sold munitions to the Allies freely; the anachronism borrows the story of the Second World War.
parts.n: KC-7.3.II.A (topic 7.5), skill 5.B. Thinking: use the excerpt's own dating of the German decision to explain the timing of entry. Trap: (B) knows that Russia's exit mattered to the war and places it before April 1917.

parts.q:
The excerpt would be most useful to a historian studying which of the following?
(A) How the president justified breaking with the tradition of staying out of European wars
(B) How strongly the American public supported entering the war in the spring of 1917
(C) How much the American Expeditionary Forces contributed to the Allied victory in 1918
(D) Why the Senate later refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles and join the League of Nations
parts.a: (A). A war message is the president's case to Congress and the public: it frames entry as defense of neutral rights and of 'democracy' and 'the rights of nations great and small,' the humanitarian and democratic principles KC-7.3.II.A describes as the justification for departing from noninvolvement. (B) A speech shows the argument used to persuade, not how many were persuaded; opinion was divided, and 6 senators and 50 representatives voted against war. (C) The address was given before any American troops fought; it cannot show their later role. (D) The phrase 'concert of free peoples' anticipates the League, but a 1917 speech cannot show the objections senators raised in 1919 and 1920.
parts.n: KC-7.3.II.A (topic 7.5), skill 2.C. Thinking: match what a presidential speech can show (its argument and purpose) to the question asked of it. Trap: (B) treats a leader's appeal as evidence of how the public responded to it.

parts.q:
A historian argues that the war Wilson described as a fight to make the world safe for democracy narrowed democratic freedoms inside the United States. Which of the following best supports this argument?
(A) The Committee on Public Information recruited thousands of speakers and artists to build public support for the war.
(B) The Selective Service Act of 1917 required millions of American men to register for a military draft.
(C) Eugene Debs, the Socialist leader, got ten years in prison under the Espionage Act for an antiwar speech.
(D) Hundreds of thousands of African Americans left the South for wartime jobs in Northern industrial cities.
parts.a: (C). Imprisoning a four-time presidential candidate for criticizing the war is direct evidence that wartime law punished political speech, the growth of official restrictions on free speech in KC-7.2.I.C. (A) Propaganda tried to persuade Americans; by itself it did not punish anyone for dissent, so it is weaker evidence than a prison sentence for a speech. (B) Conscription was a wartime obligation voted by Congress; it does not show restrictions on speech, press or political participation. (D) The Great Migration moved people toward opportunity, and migrants could vote in the North; it says nothing about wartime limits on freedom.
parts.n: KC-7.2.I.C (topic 7.6), skill 3.D. Thinking: choose the evidence that shows the claim directly rather than evidence merely about wartime pressure. Trap: (A) treats government propaganda as proof of repression without evidence that dissent was punished.

mc.stem:
Questions 10-12 refer to the excerpt below.

A lifelong resident told us that there was no need to study the whole city to learn what was changing it: the answer could be spelled in four letters, A-U-T-O. In 1890 no one here owned an automobile; by 1924 cars were common in working-class as well as business-class homes, and many were bought on time payments. Some families that owned a car still lived in a house without a bathtub, and a working-class mother of nine told us that the family would go without clothes before it would give up the car. The car has pulled leisure out of the home. Parents complain that their sons and daughters take the car and go, and that they no longer know where their children spend the evening. Ministers complain that families who once filled the pews now drive into the country on Sunday. The motion pictures, which the city's young people attend in large numbers, teach them styles of dress and courtship that their parents never knew.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from Robert S. Lynd and Helen Merrell Lynd, Middletown: A Study in Contemporary American Culture (1929), a study of Muncie, Indiana, based on fieldwork in 1924 and 1925. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q:
The excerpt's details about how working-class families in Muncie acquired and valued their cars best support which of the following conclusions about the consumer economy of the 1920s?
(A) Families stretched their budgets and took on debt to buy new goods, so spending rested partly on credit.
(B) Rising wages let working families afford every modern comfort, so cars came after homes were modernized.
(C) Working families bought cars chiefly to get to their factory jobs, so the car served work more than leisure.
(D) Mass production had made cars so cheap that owning one no longer strained a working-class family's budget.
parts.a: (A). The Lynds report that many cars were 'bought on time payments,' that some car-owning families still lived without a bathtub, and that a working-class mother of nine would give up clothes before she gave up the car. Families were stretching thin budgets and borrowing to buy a prized new good, the installment-driven consumer economy of KC-7.1.I.A. (B) The families with a car but no bathtub show the opposite: the car came before basic home comforts, not after them. (C) The excerpt stresses leisure: the car 'pulled leisure out of the home,' carried young people off in the evening and families to the country on Sunday; it says nothing about driving to work. (D) The assembly line did bring prices down, but a family that bought on installments and would 'go without clothes' to keep its car was plainly straining to own one; this choice puts a remembered fact in place of the source's evidence.
parts.n: KC-7.1.I.A and KC-7.2.I.A (topic 7.7), skill 5.B. Thinking: draw a conclusion from the source's details about how families paid for and valued their cars, not from a remembered generalization. Trap: (D) recalls that the assembly line made cars cheap and misses the source's evidence that owning one still strained working-class budgets.

parts.q:
A historian plans to cite the excerpt as evidence of how the automobile changed family life across the United States in the 1920s. Which of the following is the most important limitation of the source for that purpose?
(A) It was written after the stock market crash of 1929, so it reflects the gloom of the early Depression.
(B) Its authors quote only business leaders, who had a financial stake in the sale of automobiles.
(C) It relies on what residents told the researchers, so it can reveal nothing about how people behaved.
(D) It studies one small Midwestern city, chosen partly because few residents were immigrants or Black.
parts.a: (D). The Lynds picked Muncie because it seemed typical in some ways and because its population was overwhelmingly native-born and white, which made change easier to study; the same choice means it cannot stand for immigrant neighborhoods in big cities, the rural South, or Black communities, so national conclusions need other evidence. (A) The source line dates the fieldwork to 1924 and 1925, well before the crash; the book describes the prosperity decade from inside it. (B) The excerpt quotes a working-class mother, parents and ministers, and the ministers' complaint cuts against the car; this misreads the source. (C) Interviews have limits, but they are strong evidence of what residents did and worried about; the claim that they reveal nothing overstates the problem.
parts.n: KC-7.1.I.A and KC-7.2.I.A (topic 7.7), skill 2.C. Thinking: ask whom a local study leaves out before using it to generalize about a nation. Trap: (A) assumes any book published in 1929 was shaped by the crash, without reading the fieldwork dates.

parts.q:
The concerns of parents and ministers described in the excerpt most closely resemble the concerns that motivated which of the following groups in the 1920s?
(A) Supporters of the National Origins Act, which cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe
(B) Supporters of laws that banned the teaching of evolution in Tennessee's public schools
(C) Supporters of the Equal Rights Amendment, which Alice Paul's party first proposed in 1923
(D) Supporters of Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association in northern cities
parts.a: (B). The parents and ministers fear that a new technology and new amusements are pulling children away from church and parental authority. Supporters of the 1925 Tennessee law behind the Scopes trial feared that modern science taught in schools would do the same to children's faith: both defend traditional religion and family authority against modern culture (KC-7.2.I.D). (A) Nativists also reacted against change, but they blamed outsiders; the parents and ministers are worried about their own native-born children and new consumer habits, not about foreigners. (C) ERA supporters wanted to change women's legal position; the parents and ministers are defending older customs, the opposite impulse. (D) Garvey's followers were building racial pride and economic independence among Black migrants; their cause was not anxiety about cars and movies eroding church and home.
parts.n: KC-7.2.I.D (topic 7.8), skill 4.B. Thinking: match the underlying fear (modern culture versus traditional religion and family), not just the fact of reacting to change. Trap: (A) sees "reaction against change" in both and misses that nativists blamed foreigners, not modern culture.

mc.stem:
Questions 13-15 refer to the excerpt below.

In this country a handful of men have gathered into their own hands most of the wealth that the whole people produced, while millions who did the work go hungry and ragged. The founders declared that all men are created equal, and Scripture teaches that the fruits of the earth were given to all. It is not that there is too little; there is too much for a few and too little for the many. I propose that the law put a ceiling on the great fortunes and that the government take the surplus. From it let every family be guaranteed a homestead worth about five thousand dollars, enough for a home, an automobile and a radio, and a decent yearly income. Let the old receive pensions, let the hours of labor be cut so that all may work, and let every able child be educated through college.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from Senator Huey P. Long of Louisiana, 'Every Man a King,' a national radio address of February 23, 1934, and the Share Our Wealth program he promoted in 1934 and 1935. His Share Our Wealth Society claimed millions of members. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q:
Long's explanation of the hard times of the 1930s rests most directly on which argument about the causes of the Great Depression?
(A) Speculators had bid stock prices far above the real value of the companies behind them.
(B) High tariffs had provoked other nations to close their markets to American goods.
(C) Wealth was so unequally shared that most people could not buy what the economy made.
(D) The Federal Reserve had let the supply of money shrink as thousands of banks failed.
parts.a: (C). 'There is too much for a few and too little for the many' is the underconsumption argument: income concentrated at the top left workers and farmers unable to buy the goods that factories and farms could produce. Long's cure, redistribution, follows from that diagnosis. (A) Speculation and the 1929 crash are real causes that historians cite, but Long's excerpt never mentions the stock market; it blames the division of wealth. (B) The Hawley-Smoot Tariff (1930) and foreign retaliation deepened the slump, but nothing in the excerpt concerns trade. (D) Bank failures and the contraction of the money supply are central to some historians' account, but Long does not argue from money or banking here.
parts.n: KC-7.1.I.C and KC-7.1.III (topic 7.9), skill 5.B. Thinking: translate a political speech into the economic argument it rests on, and set aside true causes the speaker did not use. Trap: (A) answers with the cause of the Depression they know best rather than the one the source argues.

parts.q:
A historian argues that movements such as Long's pushed Franklin Roosevelt toward more far-reaching reforms. Which of the following best supports this argument?
(A) In March 1933 Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act within days of Franklin Roosevelt's inauguration as president.
(B) In 1935 the Supreme Court struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act in the Schechter Poultry case.
(C) In 1936 Roosevelt won reelection in a landslide over the Republican candidate, Governor Alf Landon of Kansas.
(D) In 1935 Roosevelt sought higher taxes on the largest incomes and estates, a bill critics called 'soak the rich.'
parts.a: (D). The Revenue Act of 1935, the 'wealth tax,' came in the year the Share Our Wealth clubs were at their height and borrowed Long's theme of taxing great fortunes; together with Social Security it marks the turn KC-7.1.III.B attributes to radical and populist pressure. (A) The banking law came a year before Long launched Share Our Wealth, so it cannot show a response to his movement. (B) Schechter did push Roosevelt toward new legislation, but it was a conservative check on the New Deal, the other half of KC-7.1.III.B, not pressure from populist movements. (C) The landslide shows the New Deal was popular; it is an outcome, not evidence that populist pressure changed what Roosevelt proposed.
parts.n: KC-7.1.III.B (topic 7.10), skill 3.D. Thinking: check that the evidence comes after the pressure and matches its content. Trap: (B) knows Schechter preceded the Second New Deal and forgets that the claim is about pressure from the left.

parts.q:
A historian wants to measure how much support Long's program had among American voters in 1935. Which of the following sources would be most useful?
(A) A private 1935 poll for the Democratic Party of how many votes Long could win as a third-party candidate
(B) The Share Our Wealth Society's own announcements of how many members had joined its clubs across the nation
(C) The texts of the radio speeches Long delivered in 1935 to promote the Share Our Wealth plan
(D) The speeches in which Roosevelt's allies attacked Long as a dangerous demagogue in 1935
parts.a: (A). An independent sample of voters taken by his rivals, who had every reason to measure his strength accurately rather than inflate it, comes closest to showing how many Americans backed him. (B) The movement's own membership claims were publicity; Long had every reason to inflate them, so they cannot be trusted as a measure without corroboration. (C) More speeches show what Long argued, not how many people agreed with him. (D) Attacks by opponents show that the administration took Long seriously, not how many voters supported him.
parts.n: KC-7.1.III.B (topic 7.10), skill 2.C. Thinking: choose a source whose author had a reason to measure support accurately. Trap: (B) takes a movement's own count of its members as a neutral measure of support.

mc.stem:
Questions 16-18 refer to the excerpt below.

The present reign of terror and international lawlessness began a few years ago. Without a declaration of war and without warning or justification, civilians, including women and children, are being ruthlessly killed by bombs from the air. Nations are interfering in the internal affairs of others and violating solemn treaties. Let no one imagine that America will escape, that this Western Hemisphere will not be attacked. The epidemic of world lawlessness is spreading. When an epidemic of physical disease starts to spread, the community approves and joins in a quarantine of the patients in order to protect the health of the community. We are determined to keep out of war, yet we cannot insure ourselves against the disastrous effects of war and the dangers of involvement. America hates war. America hopes for peace. Therefore America actively engages in the search for peace.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from President Franklin D. Roosevelt, speech in Chicago, October 5, 1937. The speech named no nation and proposed no specific measure. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q:
Roosevelt's choice to describe a 'quarantine' without naming any nation or proposing any specific measure is best explained by which of the following?
(A) His belief that the aggressor nations posed no real threat to the security of the Western Hemisphere
(B) Strong isolationist opinion, written into the Neutrality Acts that Congress passed from 1935 to 1937
(C) The Senate's rejection of the League of Nations, which barred presidents from making any foreign commitments
(D) The League of Nations' success in using economic sanctions to halt Italy's conquest of Ethiopia
parts.a: (B). Congress had passed three Neutrality Acts in three years, and polls and the press showed most Americans determined to stay out of foreign wars (KC-7.3.II.E). A president facing that opinion could warn in general terms and test the reaction, but not commit the country to act; hence 'We are determined to keep out of war.' (A) The speech itself contradicts this: 'Let no one imagine that America will escape, that this Western Hemisphere will not be attacked.' (C) The Senate's vote in 1919-1920 kept the United States out of the League, but it placed no legal bar on later presidents; it reflects the same isolationist tradition without explaining the caution of 1937. (D) The League's sanctions on Italy were weak and failed; Italy completed its conquest in 1936. A success would have made American caution less necessary, not more.
parts.n: KC-7.3.II.E (topic 7.11), skill 4.B. Thinking: explain a speaker's caution by the political limits he faced at the moment he spoke. Trap: (C) turns the isolationist tradition behind the League vote into a legal ban on presidential action.

parts.q:
A historian argues that by the time of this speech Roosevelt had decided to lead the United States into war against the aggressor nations. Which of the following developments of 1937-1938 would most seriously challenge this argument?
(A) In 1938 Roosevelt asked Congress for a large expansion of the navy, and Congress voted to approve the request.
(B) Isolationist newspapers and members of Congress attacked the Chicago speech as a step toward war.
(C) In the Munich agreement of 1938, Britain and France let Germany annex part of Czechoslovakia.
(D) After Japanese planes sank the U.S. gunboat Panay in December 1937, Roosevelt accepted Japan's apology.
parts.a: (D). Japan's aircraft sank an American warship in China two months after the speech, a ready pretext for war, and Roosevelt accepted Japan's apology and payment of damages instead. A president set on war would hardly pass up such an incident; his restraint fits KC-7.3.II.E, which notes that most Americans opposed military action until Pearl Harbor. (A) Naval expansion is consistent with preparing for war, so it supports the historian's argument more than it challenges it. (B) Attacks by critics show what opponents feared Roosevelt intended; they are evidence about the critics, not about Roosevelt's decision. (C) Munich was a British and French decision; it says nothing about what Roosevelt had decided.
parts.n: KC-7.3.II.E (topic 7.11), skill 3.D. Thinking: look for what the president did when he had a chance to act on the supposed decision. Trap: (B) takes critics' fears about Roosevelt's intentions as evidence of those intentions.

parts.q:
The approach suggested by the image of a quarantine differed from the Neutrality Acts of 1935-1937 chiefly in that it would
(A) treat aggressors differently from their victims instead of restricting all warring nations alike
(B) commit American troops to defend any nation that Germany, Italy or Japan might invade in the future
(C) end American sales of arms and loans of money to every nation that was fighting a war
(D) leave the work of stopping aggression to the League of Nations instead of to American action
parts.a: (A). The Neutrality Acts' arms embargo and limits on loans applied to every belligerent, invader and invaded alike; a quarantine isolates only the 'patients', the lawbreaking nations. That distinction between aggressor and victim is the departure, and it foreshadows cash-and-carry and Lend-Lease. (B) The speech says 'We are determined to keep out of war'; reading the quarantine as a promise of troops overstates it. (C) This describes the Neutrality Acts themselves, not the way the quarantine idea departed from them. (D) The United States was not a League member, and the speech says America 'actively engages in the search for peace'; it does not hand the task to the League.
parts.n: KC-7.3.II.E (topic 7.11), skill 3.C. Thinking: compare two policies by what each does to aggressors and to victims. Trap: (B) hears "quarantine" as a call for war and ignores the speech's pledge to keep out of it.

mc.stem:
Questions 19-21 refer to the table below.

Immigrants admitted to the United States for permanent residence, by decade (approximate figures, rounded to the nearest ten thousand)
Decade · From all countries · From Mexico
1910-1919 · 6,350,000 · 190,000
1920-1929 · 4,300,000 · 500,000
1930-1939 · 700,000 · 30,000
1940-1949 · 860,000 · 60,000

Rounded approximations compiled for this exercise from the Department of Homeland Security, Yearbook of Immigration Statistics (persons obtaining permanent resident status, by country of last residence). The table counts only immigrants admitted to stay. It does not count the Mexican contract workers (braceros) whom the United States and Mexico agreed in 1942 to bring in temporarily for farm work and, from 1943, railroad work.

parts.q:
Between the 1910s and the 1920s, immigration from all countries fell while immigration from Mexico more than doubled. Which of the following best explains this contrast?
(A) The First World War disrupted Atlantic shipping, keeping European emigrants at home through the 1920s.
(B) The Great Migration of Black Southerners to the North left the farms of the Southwest short of workers.
(C) Quota laws limited immigrants from Europe and Asia but set no quotas for Western Hemisphere nations.
(D) The bracero agreement recruited Mexican farmworkers to take the place of the European immigrants.
parts.a: (C). The quota acts of 1921 and 1924 slashed arrivals from southern and eastern Europe and barred most Asians, lowering the total (KC-7.2.II.A.ii); because they set no quotas for the Americas, employers in the Southwest and the Midwest turned to Mexican workers, and Mexican immigration rose. Only this explains both halves of the contrast. (A) The war cut Atlantic crossings from 1914 to 1918, which lowered the 1910s figure, not the 1920s one; after 1918 Europeans could sail again, and the quotas, not the war, held them back. (B) The Great Migration drew people from the Southeast to Northern cities; it did not empty Southwestern farms, and it cannot explain why total immigration fell. (D) The bracero agreement dates from 1942, and the note says braceros are not counted in the table at all.
parts.n: KC-7.2.II.A.ii and KC-7.2.II.D (topic 7.8), skill 5.B. Thinking: find the one development that explains both the fall in the total and the rise from Mexico. Trap: (A) links the war to lower European immigration without checking which decade the war falls in.

parts.q:
Which of the following best explains the change in immigration from Mexico between the 1920s and the 1930s shown in the table?
(A) The end of the fighting in the Mexican Revolution, which removed the main reason to leave Mexico
(B) Mass unemployment in the Depression, and local and federal drives that pressed Mexicans to leave
(C) The Dust Bowl, which destroyed the Southwestern farms where most Mexican immigrants had found work
(D) An export boom in Mexico, which offered better wages to workers who chose to stay at home
parts.a: (B). When jobs vanished after 1929, few Mexicans came, and officials and relief agencies pressed hundreds of thousands of Mexican immigrants and Mexican American citizens to return to Mexico (repatriation). The same government recruited Mexican workers a decade later: the contradictory policy of KC-7.2.II.D. (A) The table undercuts this: the Revolution's main fighting was over by 1920, yet the 1920s were the peak decade for Mexican immigration. (C) The Dust Bowl ruined farms on the southern Great Plains, not the irrigated fields of California and south Texas where many Mexicans worked, so the premise of this choice is false. (D) The Depression hit Mexico's exports too; there was no boom to draw workers home.
parts.n: KC-7.2.II.D (topic 7.12), skill 5.B. Thinking: match a sharp change in the data to the economic and political conditions of that decade. Trap: (C) reaches for the best-known migration story of the 1930s without checking where and when it happened.

parts.q:
A student concludes from the table that the Second World War did little to increase the number of Mexican workers coming to the United States. Which of the following best evaluates the student's conclusion?
(A) It is sound, because Mexican immigration in the 1940s stayed far below its level in the 1920s.
(B) It is sound, because the war closed the border and cut most travel between Mexico and the United States.
(C) It is flawed, because the table shows that most immigrants of the 1940s came from Mexico.
(D) It is flawed, because the table leaves out the braceros recruited for wartime farm and rail jobs.
parts.a: (D). The note says the table counts only permanent immigrants. Wartime Mexican labor came mainly through the bracero agreements of 1942 and 1943, which brought workers in on temporary contracts to replace farm and railroad workers drawn into the armed forces and war plants, so the table cannot measure the change the student asks about. (A) The student reads the numbers correctly but ignores what the table counts; a source cannot rule out what it was never designed to measure. (B) Mexico joined the Allies in 1942 and cooperated in sending workers north; the border was not closed. (C) About 60,000 of 860,000 immigrants in the 1940s came from Mexico, well under a tenth; this misreads the table.
parts.n: KC-7.2.II.D and KC-7.3.III.C.i (topic 7.12), skill 2.C. Thinking: test a conclusion against what the data set actually counts. Trap: (A) trusts the numbers without reading the note on what they leave out.

mc.stem:
Questions 22-25 refer to the two excerpts below.

Source 1
My chief purpose was to end the war in victory with the least possible cost in the lives of the men in the armies I had helped to raise. The Japanese army was still strong, and our plans called for an invasion of the home islands beginning in November 1945. I was informed that such operations might be expected to cost over a million casualties to American forces alone. At no time from 1941 to 1945 did I hear it suggested by the President, or by any other responsible member of the government, that atomic energy should not be used in the war. The decision to use the bomb was the least abhorrent choice open to us.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from Henry L. Stimson, secretary of war from 1940 to 1945, 'The Decision to Use the Atomic Bomb,' Harper's Magazine, February 1947. The wording is not a direct quotation.

Source 2
By the summer of 1945 American leaders knew from intercepted Japanese messages that Tokyo was looking for a way out of the war, and a Soviet declaration of war on Japan, expected in August, promised to deliver a heavy blow. The bomb was not needed to avoid an invasion that was still months away. Its use is better explained by the diplomacy of the coming peace: American leaders hoped that the new weapon would end the war before the Soviet Union could claim a large role in the Asian settlement, and would make Moscow more cooperative in Europe.

Paraphrase of the argument in Gar Alperovitz, Atomic Diplomacy: Hiroshima and Potsdam (1965), condensed for this exercise. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q:
Which of the following most limits the usefulness of Source 1 as evidence of why American leaders used the atomic bomb?
(A) It appeared in a popular magazine, so Stimson could draw on nothing from official records.
(B) Stimson left office before the bombs were used, so he could only repeat what others told him.
(C) Stimson wrote it in 1947 as a public defense of a decision that he had helped to make.
(D) Historians dispute his casualty figure, which proves that his account of his own motives is false.
parts.a: (C). Stimson chaired the committee that advised Truman on the bomb, and he wrote this article two years later, as criticism of the bombings grew after John Hersey's Hiroshima appeared in 1946. A participant's public justification, written with hindsight, is strong evidence of the official case but weaker evidence of every motive at the time. (A) Writing for a mass audience does not bar the use of records; Stimson drew on his diary and papers. The audience matters for purpose, not for access. (B) Stimson was secretary of war until September 1945, after Japan's surrender, and was at the center of the decision. (D) A disputed estimate weakens part of his case, but it does not prove what his motives were; the reasoning jumps from one doubtful number to a verdict on the whole account.
parts.n: KC-7.3.III.D (topic 7.13), skill 2.C. Thinking: weigh the author's role, date and purpose against the question the historian is asking. Trap: (D) treats doubt about one figure as proof that the whole account is false.

parts.q:
Source 2's argument depends most on which feature of the diplomatic situation in the summer of 1945?
(A) At Yalta, Stalin had promised to join the war on Japan about three months after Germany's defeat.
(B) The Soviet Union had signed a neutrality pact with Japan in 1941 and fully intended to keep it.
(C) The Potsdam Declaration had promised Japan that it could keep its emperor after it surrendered.
(D) Britain and the United States had opened a second front against Germany in France in 1944.
parts.a: (A). Germany surrendered on May 8, 1945, and the Yalta promise put Soviet entry about three months later: early August. That deadline is what gives Source 2's argument its force; the Soviet Union declared war on Japan on August 8, between the two bombs. (B) The pact of April 1941 was real, but the Soviets had already promised at Yalta to enter the Pacific war; if they meant to stay neutral, Source 2's timetable would make no sense. (C) The Potsdam Declaration of July 26, 1945 demanded unconditional surrender and said nothing about the emperor, an omission historians still debate. (D) The D-Day landing is true but concerns the European war; it does not bear on Soviet entry into the war in Asia.
parts.n: KC-7.3.III.E and KC-7.3.III.D (topic 7.14), skill 4.B. Thinking: identify the diplomatic fact an argument takes for granted. Trap: (B) remembers the Soviet-Japanese neutrality pact and misses that the Soviets had promised at Yalta to break it.

parts.q:
Which of the following, if presented by a historian, would most weaken the argument in Source 2?
(A) Intercepted cables in July 1945 showed Japan's foreign minister asking Moscow to help end the war.
(B) Truman grew more confident in his talks with Stalin at Potsdam once he learned of the successful atomic test.
(C) Some of the scientists who built the bomb petitioned against using it on Japanese cities without warning.
(D) After both bombs and the Soviet attack, Japan's war council stayed deadlocked until the emperor intervened.
parts.a: (D). On August 9, after Hiroshima, the Soviet declaration and Nagasaki, Japan's leaders still split evenly over surrender; only the emperor's intervention broke the deadlock, and army officers then tried to stop the surrender by force. If Japan resisted this long even after the bombs, the claim that it was nearly ready to quit without them is much weaker. (A) These cables are the intercepted messages Source 2 relies on; they support the argument rather than weaken it. (B) A president emboldened in dealing with Stalin fits Source 2's picture of the bomb as a diplomatic lever; it does not weaken it. (C) The petition shows moral doubts among scientists, but it says nothing about how close Japan was to surrender or what moved the leaders who decided.
parts.n: KC-7.3.III.D (topic 7.13), skill 6.D. Thinking: find evidence that attacks the argument's key premise (Japan was ready to surrender) rather than evidence on a side issue. Trap: (C) sees evidence of opposition to the bomb and assumes it must weaken the case for it.

parts.q:
Both sources assume which of the following?
(A) An American invasion of Japan's home islands would have begun in August 1945 if the bomb had not been used.
(B) Using the bomb would make Japan surrender sooner than it would have surrendered without the bomb.
(C) Senior members of the government had urged the President not to use the bomb against Japan.
(D) The Soviet Union had become the main threat to American security by the summer of 1945.
parts.a: (B). Source 1 defends the bomb as the way to end the war at least cost; Source 2 says leaders hoped it would end the war before the Soviets could claim a large role. Both take for granted that the bomb would hasten Japan's surrender (KC-7.3.III.D); they disagree about why leaders wanted that. (A) Source 1 dates the invasion to November and Source 2 calls it 'months away'; neither assumes an August invasion. (C) Source 1 says the opposite: no responsible official suggested not using it. Source 2 does not address the point. (D) Source 2 implies concern about Soviet influence, but Source 1 never mentions the Soviet Union; an assumption of one source is not shared.
parts.n: KC-7.3.III.D (topic 7.13), skill 3.C. Thinking: find the premise both arguments need even though they disagree about motive. Trap: (D) carries one source's view into the other.

fr.title: The New Deal: transformation or rescue?
fr.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the two excerpts below.

Historian A
The New Deal was a halfway revolution. It left the great corporations in place and did little for sharecroppers, farmworkers or most African Americans. Yet it changed the relationship between Americans and their government for good. Before 1933 Washington took little responsibility for the jobless, the old or the unorganized worker; by 1938 the federal government was expected to steady the economy, to guarantee a minimum of security to its citizens, and to protect the right of workers to organize. A government that had answered mainly to business now had to answer to farmers, workers and other organized groups as well.

Paraphrase of the argument in William E. Leuchtenburg, Franklin D. Roosevelt and the New Deal, 1932-1940 (1963), condensed for this exercise. The wording is not a direct quotation.

Historian B
The reforms of the New Deal were conservative achievements. They saved corporate capitalism rather than changing it. Relief and recovery programs helped most those who already had some economic or political power, while the poorest Americans, including sharecroppers and most Black workers, were left out or pushed aside. Wealth was not significantly redistributed, and power over the economy stayed with those who had held it before 1933. The New Deal's great accomplishment was to restore confidence in the system whose failure had caused the crisis.

Paraphrase of the argument in Barton J. Bernstein, 'The New Deal: The Conservative Achievements of Liberal Reform,' in Towards a New Past (1968), condensed for this exercise. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q: Briefly describe ONE major difference between Historian A's and Historian B's interpretations of the New Deal.
parts.a: Historian A argues that, despite its limits, the New Deal permanently changed the role of the federal government, making it responsible for economic security, the jobless and the right to organize. Historian B argues that it changed little of substance: it rescued corporate capitalism, left power and wealth where they were, and helped the already powerful more than the poor. Both note that sharecroppers and Black workers were left out; they differ on whether the New Deal's changes were fundamental.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'A likes the New Deal and B does not', or a summary of one historian only. Saying they disagree about whether the poor were left out is wrong: both say so.

parts.q: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical development from 1933 to 1940, not mentioned in the excerpts, could be used to support Historian B's interpretation.
parts.a: The Agricultural Adjustment Act (1933) supports Historian B. It paid landowners to take land out of production, and many owners kept the payments and evicted tenants and sharecroppers, many of them Black, so a New Deal program aided those with property and pushed the poorest off the land. (Also accepted, if explained: the Emergency Banking Act of 1933 reopened private banks rather than nationalizing them; Federal Housing Administration rules that denied loans in Black neighborhoods; the NRA codes written largely by the biggest firms in each industry.)
parts.n: Earns nothing: evidence that only shows the New Deal did something (for example, 'the WPA hired millions'), which supports A as easily as B; or a development named without explaining how it shows the powerful gained or the poor were left out. Social Security's exclusions are acceptable here only if not reused in (c).

parts.q: A student argues that the Social Security Act of 1935 proves that Historian A is right and Historian B is wrong. Evaluate the student's argument, explaining how the act can be used as evidence for one or both interpretations.
parts.a: The student is only partly right, because the act supports both historians. It supports Historian A: for the first time the federal government took lasting responsibility for old-age pensions and, with the states, unemployment insurance, the new relationship between citizens and Washington that A describes. It also supports Historian B: it left out agricultural and domestic workers, the jobs held by most Black workers in the South, and it was paid for by a flat payroll tax on workers and employers rather than by taxing wealth, so it did little to redistribute income. The act shows a real change in the government's role within the limits B describes.
parts.n: Earns nothing: simply agreeing ('Social Security helped the elderly, so A is right') without testing the claim against B, or disagreeing without evidence from the act itself. The point requires using a feature of the act to address the student's 'proves'.

fr.title: Du Bois's 'Returning Soldiers': a turn after the war
fr.stem:
Answer (a), (b), and (c) using the excerpt below.

We are coming home from the war. For France we fought gladly and to the last drop of blood; for America and her highest ideals we fought in far-off hope. This is our fatherland, and it was right for us to fight. But it is a shameful land. It lynches. It disfranchises its own citizens. It encourages ignorance among us. It steals from us. It insults us. Now that the war is over, we must marshal every ounce of our strength to fight a sterner, longer battle against the forces of hell in our own land. We return. We return from fighting. We return fighting. Make way for Democracy! We saved it in France, and by the Great Jehovah, we will save it in the United States of America, or know the reason why.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from W. E. B. Du Bois, 'Returning Soldiers,' an editorial in The Crisis, the magazine of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, May 1919. The last five sentences are Du Bois's own words; the rest is not a direct quotation.

parts.q: Briefly describe the historical situation in which Du Bois wrote this editorial.
parts.a: Du Bois wrote as Black soldiers came home from the First World War, in which they had served in segregated units in a war that Wilson said would make the world safe for democracy. At home, lynching continued, Southern states still disfranchised Black voters, and the Great Migration had brought hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners to Northern cities, where competition for jobs and housing had already produced violence such as the East St. Louis riot of 1917.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'it was after World War I' with no description, or context from the wrong time (the civil rights movement of the 1950s). The Chicago riot of July 1919 came after the editorial, so it cannot be context for it, though it can be used in (b).

parts.q: Briefly explain ONE specific way African Americans acted on the attitude expressed in the excerpt between 1919 and 1930.
parts.a: During the riots of the 'Red Summer' of 1919, in Chicago and Washington, Black residents, including veterans, fought back against white mobs rather than submitting, the 'return fighting' Du Bois called for. (Also accepted, if explained: the NAACP's campaign for the Dyer anti-lynching bill, which passed the House in 1922; the 'New Negro' of the Harlem Renaissance, whose writers such as Claude McKay ('If We Must Die', 1919) and Langston Hughes asserted Black pride and equality; the mass following of Marcus Garvey's UNIA.)
parts.n: Earns nothing: naming the Harlem Renaissance or the NAACP without explaining how it expressed demands for rights and self-assertion; examples from after 1930, such as the March on Washington Movement of 1941.

parts.q: In July 1918 Du Bois had urged African Americans in The Crisis to 'close ranks' with white Americans and set aside their grievances while the war lasted. Briefly explain ONE reason for the change in his tone by May 1919, and support your answer with evidence.
parts.a: Du Bois had hoped that loyal wartime service would earn Black Americans equal treatment; by 1919 that hope had failed. Black soldiers had been segregated, mostly assigned to labor battalions, and treated with contempt by their own army in France, and at home lynchings continued through 1918 and 1919, including of Black men in uniform. With the war over, there was no longer a reason to postpone grievances, and the gap between Wilson's democratic war aims and Black Americans' treatment made the change of tone a demand for the democracy they had fought for.
parts.n: Earns nothing: 'he changed his mind' or 'he got angry' without a reason; a reason with no evidence; or a reason that confuses the two dates (for example, citing the 1919 riots that came after May as the cause).

fr.title: U.S. foreign policy from 1898 to 1941: how much changed?
fr.stem:
Evaluate the extent to which the United States' role in world affairs changed from the Spanish-American War of 1898 to the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941.

In your response, develop an argument that evaluates the extent of change and continuity, supported by specific evidence from the period.

rows.earns: A historically defensible claim about extent that sets up a line of reasoning, e.g.: 'Although the United States moved from acquiring an overseas empire in 1898 to rejecting the League of Nations and passing neutrality laws in the 1930s, its role changed less than it seemed: throughout the period it intervened freely in the Western Hemisphere and pursued trade in Asia while refusing binding commitments in Europe, until the war in Europe and Asia forced it to abandon neutrality in 1940 and 1941.'
rows.loses: 'U.S. foreign policy changed a lot between 1898 and 1941' with no weighing of change against continuity; a claim about one event only (the Spanish-American War); a thesis that simply restates the prompt.

rows.earns: Describes a broader development and ties it to the prompt, e.g.: the industrial growth of the late nineteenth century, the search for foreign markets after the depression of the 1890s, the sense that the frontier had closed, Mahan's arguments for sea power, and the European scramble for colonies, which together pushed the United States toward overseas expansion in 1898.
rows.loses: A phrase such as 'imperialism was popular' or 'World War II was happening' with no description; context unrelated to foreign policy.

rows.earns: 2 points: at least two specific, relevant pieces of evidence used to support an argument about change or continuity, e.g.: annexation of the Philippines and the Philippine-American War (1899-1902); the Open Door notes (1899-1900); the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) and interventions in the Caribbean; entry into the First World War (1917); the Senate's rejection of the Treaty of Versailles (1919-1920); the Washington Naval Conference (1921-1922) and the Dawes Plan (1924); the Good Neighbor Policy (1933); the Neutrality Acts (1935-1937); cash-and-carry (1939), the destroyers-for-bases deal (1940) and Lend-Lease (1941). 1 point: identifies at least two pieces of relevant evidence without using them to support an argument. A line that earns 2: 'The Good Neighbor Policy's withdrawal of Marines from Haiti in 1934 marked a real change from the Roosevelt Corollary's interventions, but the same years' Neutrality Acts continued the refusal of European commitments that had defeated the League.'
rows.loses: A list of events with no link to change or continuity; evidence from outside the period (the Monroe Doctrine alone, the Marshall Plan); vague references such as 'the U.S. helped in World War I'.

rows.earns: 1 point: uses continuity and change to frame the argument, e.g., explaining why the retreat from Europe after 1920 did not mean withdrawal from the world. 2 points: also shows a complex understanding, e.g., distinguishing the Western Hemisphere and Asia, where the United States acted freely, from Europe, where it avoided alliances; explaining that 1920s 'isolationism' coexisted with active economic diplomacy such as the Dawes Plan; weighing both change and continuity; or explaining how different groups (business interests, anti-imperialists, progressives, isolationists) shaped each shift.
rows.loses: Narrating events in order with no argument about extent; a single sentence of 'complexity' added at the end; treating the period as simple isolationism or simple expansion without accounting for counter-evidence.

u8.intro: Every excerpt is paraphrased and labelled with its source, and the table gives rounded figures. Answer from the sources and from what you know of the period 1945 to 1980.

mc.stem:
Questions 1-4 refer to the two excerpts below.

Source 1
Let every nation know, whether it wishes us well or ill, that we shall pay any price, bear any burden, meet any hardship, support any friend, oppose any foe, in order to assure the survival and the success of liberty. To the new states that we welcome to the ranks of the free, we pledge our word that one form of colonial control shall not pass away merely to be replaced by a far more iron tyranny. To our sister republics south of our border, we offer a new alliance for progress, to help free men and free governments cast off the chains of poverty.

President John F. Kennedy, inaugural address, January 20, 1961. The first sentence is Kennedy's own words; the rest is paraphrased and condensed for this exercise.

Source 2
First, the United States will keep all of its treaty commitments. Second, we shall provide a shield if a nuclear power threatens the freedom of a nation allied with us or of a nation whose survival we consider vital to our security. Third, in cases involving other types of aggression, we shall furnish military and economic assistance when requested in accordance with our treaty commitments. But we shall look to the nation directly threatened to assume the primary responsibility of providing the manpower for its defense.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from President Richard M. Nixon, televised address on the war in Vietnam, November 3, 1969, restating the policy he had first announced on Guam that July. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q:
Which of the following best describes the change in U.S. policy from Source 1 to Source 2?
(A) From containing communism to trying to roll back Communist governments already in power in Eastern Europe
(B) From an open-ended pledge to defend liberty anywhere to a policy that asked allies to supply the soldiers
(C) From reliance on nuclear weapons to reliance on economic aid as the main tool for resisting communism
(D) From alliances with newly independent nations to a withdrawal from all American treaty commitments abroad
parts.a: (B). Kennedy promises to 'pay any price, bear any burden' with no limit on American effort; Nixon keeps the commitments and the aid but says the threatened nation must provide 'the manpower for its defense.' The goal of containment stays; the share of the burden Americans will carry changes. (A) Neither source speaks of rolling back Communist rule; Nixon's policy narrows the American role rather than widening it. (C) Source 2 still promises a nuclear 'shield', and Source 1 already offers economic aid; the change is about who fights, not about nuclear versus economic tools. (D) Source 2 opens by promising to 'keep all of its treaty commitments'; this reads Nixon's limits as a retreat he explicitly denies.
parts.n: KC-8.1.I and KC-8.1.I.C (topic 8.2), skill 3.C. Thinking: separate what stays the same (containment, commitments) from what changes (who supplies the soldiers). Trap: (C) sees "economic assistance" in Source 2 and misses that Source 2 also keeps the nuclear shield.

parts.q:
Which of the following best explains the shift from Source 1 to Source 2?
(A) The Sino-Soviet split, which convinced Nixon that communism no longer threatened any nation in Asia
(B) The Cuban Missile Crisis, which led both superpowers to agree to reduce their nuclear arsenals
(C) The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, which drained Soviet strength and eased the danger to American allies
(D) The cost of the war in Vietnam in American lives and money, and the protest it provoked at home
parts.a: (D). By 1969 more than half a million Americans were in Vietnam, tens of thousands had died, the war fed inflation, and protest had helped drive Johnson from the 1968 race (KC-8.1.II.B). Nixon's doctrine, applied as 'Vietnamization', promised to keep containment while bringing American soldiers home. (A) The split between China and the Soviet Union was real and Nixon later exploited it, but the doctrine was announced on Guam about Asian allies precisely because he still expected Communist threats there. (B) The 1962 crisis led to a hotline and the 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty, not to cuts in arsenals; and Source 2 still relies on a nuclear shield. (C) The invasion came in December 1979, ten years after Source 2; it cannot explain a 1969 policy.
parts.n: KC-8.1.I.B.ii and KC-8.1.II.B (topic 8.8), skill 5.B. Thinking: explain a change in policy by the costs of the policy it replaced. Trap: (A) knows Nixon exploited the Sino-Soviet split and treats it as the cause of a doctrine aimed at Asia.

parts.q:
A historian argues that Source 2 marked the abandonment of the policy of containment. Which of the following most seriously challenges this argument?
(A) Nixon kept U.S. treaties in force, armed allies against Communist attack, and kept fighting in Vietnam until the 1973 peace accords.
(B) Nixon traveled to the People's Republic of China in 1972, becoming the first American president to visit the country.
(C) Nixon and the Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev signed the SALT I agreement placing limits on nuclear arms in 1972.
(D) Nixon withdrew most American ground troops from South Vietnam between his inauguration in 1969 and the end of 1972.
parts.a: (A). Containment means preventing the spread of Communist power. Nixon's doctrine keeps the treaties, the nuclear shield and military aid, and American forces kept fighting, with heavy bombing as late as December 1972, until the Paris accords of January 1973; what changed was the method (allies' manpower), not the goal. (B) Opening relations with a Communist power could look like abandoning containment, so this seems to support the historian rather than challenge the argument. (C) Arms control with the Soviet Union is détente, which can look like a retreat from containment; it does not challenge the historian. (D) Withdrawal fits the historian's reading of Source 2 as a retreat, so it supports rather than challenges the argument.
parts.n: KC-8.1.I and KC-8.1.I.C (topic 8.2), skill 3.D. Thinking: test a claim of abandonment by asking whether the goal changed or only the means. Trap: (D) takes the withdrawal of troops as proof that containment itself was dropped.

parts.q:
In the 1970s the Nixon administration sold large quantities of advanced weapons to the Shah of Iran so that Iran's own armed forces could guard the Persian Gulf against Soviet influence. This policy most directly applied which of the following ideas?
(A) Kennedy's pledge to bear any burden and meet any hardship to assure the survival of liberty
(B) Nixon's promise of a nuclear shield for allies threatened by an attack from a nuclear power
(C) Nixon's expectation that a threatened nation would supply the soldiers for its own defense
(D) Kennedy's pledge that colonial control would not be replaced by a more iron tyranny
parts.a: (C). Arming Iran so that Iranian forces, not American ones, would police the Gulf is Source 2's third point in practice: America furnishes weapons, the ally furnishes the soldiers. It extends the doctrine from Southeast Asia to the Middle East (KC-8.1.I.D.i, KC-8.1.II.D). (A) Kennedy's pledge implies an open-ended American commitment; the arms sales were designed to avoid sending Americans at all. (B) This is in Source 2, but no nuclear guarantee was involved in selling conventional weapons to Iran; it is the right source and the wrong principle. (D) That line addresses newly independent nations and names the goal of keeping them from Communist rule; it says nothing about who would do the fighting, which is what the arms sales decided.
parts.n: KC-8.1.I.D.i and KC-8.1.II.D (topic 8.7), skill 5.B. Thinking: recognize a stated principle at work in a new region and a new decade. Trap: (B) picks the Nixon Doctrine but the wrong clause of it.

mc.stem:
Questions 5-7 refer to the excerpt below.

This bill would require Communist organizations, and the groups the government judges to be their 'fronts', to register with a federal board and to list their officers and members. The Communists will not register, and the bill would do little to catch them. Its real targets would be ordinary citizens who join organizations that, without their knowledge, include Communists. It would put the government in the business of thought control, and it would be the greatest danger to freedom of speech, press and assembly since the Alien and Sedition Laws of 1798. In a free country, we punish men for the crimes they commit, but never for the opinions they have. We need not sacrifice our liberties in order to protect our security.

Paraphrased and condensed for this exercise from President Harry S. Truman, message to Congress vetoing the Internal Security Act (the McCarran Act), September 22, 1950. Congress overrode the veto by the next day, by large majorities in both houses. The wording is not a direct quotation.

parts.q:
A student concludes from the excerpt that Truman opposed efforts to remove Communists from the federal government. Which of the following best evaluates the student's conclusion?
(A) It is sound, because Truman compares the bill to the Alien and Sedition Laws, which Americans had long condemned.
(B) It is sound, because Congress had to override Truman's veto to put the Internal Security Act into effect.
(C) It is flawed, because Truman signed the bill into law once Congress amended it to answer his objections.
(D) It is flawed, because Truman had ordered loyalty investigations of all federal employees in 1947.
parts.a: (D). Truman's Executive Order 9835 (March 1947) set up loyalty boards to screen federal workers and fire those judged disloyal. His veto objects to this bill's methods, registration and guilt by association, not to the goal of keeping Communists out of government; both parties shared that goal (KC-8.1.II.A). (A) The comparison attacks this bill's threat to free speech; it says nothing about Truman's view of removing Communists from government jobs. (B) The override shows Truman opposed this particular law, not that he opposed every anticommunist measure. (C) Truman did not sign it; Congress passed it over his veto, as the source line says.
parts.n: KC-8.1.II.A (topic 8.3), skill 2.C. Thinking: distinguish opposition to a method from opposition to a goal, using what else the author did. Trap: (B) reads a veto of one law as opposition to anticommunism in general.

parts.q:
The size of the majorities by which Congress overrode Truman's veto in September 1950 is best explained by which of the following?
(A) Fears heightened by the outbreak of the Korean War that June and by recent cases of Soviet espionage
(B) The Senate's censure of Joseph McCarthy, which made its members eager to show they were not soft on communism
(C) Public alarm at the Soviet launch of Sputnik, which many blamed on spies who had stolen American secrets
(D) A Supreme Court ruling that the Communist Party was a lawful party entitled to the full protection of the law
parts.a: (A). North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, months after the Soviet atomic test and the Communist victory in China (1949), Alger Hiss's perjury conviction (January 1950) and the arrest of the Rosenbergs (summer 1950). In that climate few members of either party would vote against an internal security bill. (B) The Senate censured McCarthy in December 1954, four years after the override. (C) Sputnik went up in October 1957, seven years later; this places a Cold War shock in the wrong decade. (D) The Court ruled the other way in Dennis v. United States (1951), upholding the convictions of Communist Party leaders.
parts.n: KC-8.1.II.A and KC-8.1.I.B.i (topic 8.3), skill 4.B. Thinking: place a vote in the events of the months just before it. Trap: (B) links McCarthy to the Red Scare without checking that his censure came years later.

parts.q:
Truman's comparison of the bill to the Alien and Sedition Laws of 1798 is most apt in which of the following respects?
(A) Both measures were passed by Congress over the veto of the president who was then in office.
(B) Both measures were struck down by the Supreme Court within a few years of their passage.
(C) Both measures used fear of a foreign enemy's influence to justify restricting dissent at home.
(D) Both measures were aimed only at immigrants who had not yet become citizens of the United States.
parts.a: (C). The 1798 laws came during the Quasi-War with France and punished critics of the Adams administration as dangers to national security; the 1950 law, passed during the Korean War, treated membership in suspect groups as a security threat. In each case fear of a foreign power's agents justified limits on domestic dissent. (A) President John Adams signed the Alien and Sedition Acts; only the 1950 law was passed over a veto. (B) The Sedition Act expired in 1801 without a Supreme Court ruling, and the Court did not strike down the McCarran Act's registration rules until the 1960s. (D) The Alien Acts targeted noncitizens, but the Sedition Act punished citizens for speech, and the 1950 law's registration rules applied to citizens as well.
parts.n: KC-8.1.II.A (topic 8.3), skill 5.A. Thinking: compare two episodes across periods and find the feature they truly share. Trap: (D) remembers that the 1798 laws included Alien Acts and generalizes from the name.

mc.stem:
Questions 8-10 refer to the table below.

Population of five states, 1950-1980 (in millions, rounded to the nearest tenth)
State · 1950 · 1960 · 1970 · 1980
Arizona · 0.7 · 1.3 · 1.8 · 2.7
California · 10.6 · 15.7 · 20.0 · 23.7
Florida · 2.8 · 5.0 · 6.8 · 9.7
New York · 14.8 · 16.8 · 18.2 · 17.6
Pennsylvania · 10.5 · 11.3 · 11.8 · 11.9
United States (nearest million) · 151 · 179 · 203 · 227

Source: U.S. Census Bureau, decennial census counts, rounded for this exercise.

parts.q:
Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the table?
(A) California's rate of growth increased in each decade from 1950 to 1980 as more and more migrants arrived.
(B) Florida's population more than tripled from 1950 to 1980, while Pennsylvania's grew by under a fifth.
(C) Arizona added more residents between 1950 and 1980 than any of the other four states in the table.
(D) New York lost population in each decade after 1950 as its residents moved to the South and West.
parts.a: (B). Florida rose from 2.8 to 9.7 million, about 3.5 times its 1950 size; Pennsylvania rose from 10.5 to 11.9 million, about 13 percent. The contrast is the Sun Belt pattern of KC-8.3.I.B. (A) California added the most people, but its rate fell each decade: about 48 percent in the 1950s, 27 percent in the 1960s and 19 percent in the 1970s. (C) Arizona grew fastest in percentage terms, but it added about 2 million people; California added about 13 million. This confuses a rate with an amount. (D) New York grew in the 1950s and 1960s and lost people only in the 1970s, from 18.2 to 17.6 million.
parts.n: KC-8.3.I.B (topic 8.4), skill 5.A. Thinking: compute growth as a ratio and check each claim against every decade it covers. Trap: (A) sees California's huge numbers and assumes its growth rate was rising.

parts.q:
A student argues that the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 was the main cause of the growth of Arizona and Florida shown in the table. Which of the following best evaluates the student's argument?
(A) It is strong, because the act ended the national origins quotas, and immigration from Latin America and Asia rose sharply in the years after it.
(B) It is strong, because both states grew at a higher percentage rate in the 1970s, after the act took effect, than they had in the 1950s.
(C) It is weak, because the act kept the old quotas on immigrants from Latin America, so few of them were able to settle in either state.
(D) It is weak, because both states grew at their fastest rate in the 1950s, before the act, as defense jobs and air conditioning drew newcomers.
parts.a: (D). A cause must come before its effect. By the table, Arizona grew from 0.7 to 1.3 million in the 1950s (well over half again) and Florida from 2.8 to 5.0 million (nearly 80 percent), faster than in either later decade, and all of this came before the 1965 act. Most of the newcomers were Americans moving from other states, drawn by military bases and aerospace contracts, air conditioning, lower costs and a warm climate that attracted retirees (KC-8.3.I.A, KC-8.3.I.B). (A) Both facts are true, but they ignore the table: the growth was already rapid a decade before the act, so the act cannot be the main cause of the whole pattern. (B) The table shows the opposite: Arizona grew about 50 percent and Florida about 43 percent in the 1970s, well below their rates in the 1950s. More people were added in the 1970s, but the rate was lower. (C) The right verdict for a wrong reason: the national origins quotas never applied to the Western Hemisphere, and the 1965 act, far from keeping them, set the first overall ceiling on Western Hemisphere immigration.
parts.n: KC-8.3.I.A and KC-8.3.I.B (topic 8.4), skill 5.B. Thinking: test a causal claim against the timing the data show, computing each decade's rate of growth. Trap: (A) offers true facts about the 1965 act and never checks them against when the growth happened.

parts.q:
Seats in the House of Representatives are divided among the states after each census according to population. Which of the following best predicts how the changes shown in the table affected the division of seats after the 1980 census?
(A) Pennsylvania gained seats, because its population grew in every decade.
(B) New York lost seats, because its share of the nation's population fell.
(C) Arizona lost seats, because it remained the smallest state in the table.
(D) Every state in the table gained seats, because the national population grew.
